title: Efficient Dialect-Agnostic SQL Equivalence Refutation
summary: Identifying semantically inequivalent SQL queries is useful for many applications, such as evaluating Text-to-SQL and dialect translation systems. However, existing approaches often struggle with the diversity of SQL features and dialects, requiring significant manual effort and expertise to extend query feature support across Database Management Systems (DBMSs). To address these limitations, we present SQLWitness, an efficient, DBMS-agnostic query equivalence refutation engine. Our core idea is leveraging the DBMS execution engine to determine whether generated instances constitute counterexamples, thereby faithfully capturing the semantics of the SQL dialect and preventing false counterexamples. To efficiently generate test data, our approach explores a constrained data-generation space and uses an integrity-constraint-aware generation strategy. Furthermore, to guide time-efficient termination of this test-data generation process, we pair predicate-coverage signals with a statistical estimator. We extensively evaluated SQLWitness on six benchmark suites across four SQL dialects. SQLWitness refuted 5.34% to 88.4% more pairs than state-of-the-art baselines, and processed query pairs in 0.12 seconds on average, achieving a speedup from 2.1x to 16.4x over the baselines. Furthermore, in a case study, SQLWitness found 8.4% inconsistent translations within a dialect translation benchmark. We believe SQLWitness could be broadly adopted for many use cases.

title: The Case for TPU-Accelerated Analytical Query Processing
summary:
Large-scale analytical query processing requires computing substrates capable of immense distributed scale-out. Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) perfectly embody this extreme-scale architecture, offering massive computational density and highly scalable optical pod-level interconnects. Despite these advantages, TPUs have so far remained largely unexplored for analytical database workloads. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive case for TPU-accelerated analytical query processing by running all the TPC-H queries entirely on the TPUs. We introduce Native TPU Accelerator (NTA) for analytical query processing, which provides hardware-conscious algorithm design and optimizations in JAX/XLA. By exposing the TPU's structural mechanics, we demonstrate how dynamic, memory-bound database operations can be rewritten into deterministic JAX programs. We engineer a suite of novel execution strategies that leverage both the TPU's TensorCore and SparseCore to trade sparse, unpredictable memory accesses for dense, hardware-aligned ones. At the core of NTA, a compiler uses catalog statistics to assign guarded static capacities and a hardware-calibrated local cost model to select a TPU-native implementation for each relational operator before JIT compilation.
  We evaluate our system using the TPC-H benchmark. Taking full advantage of TPU slices and JAX distributed computing, we seamlessly scale our execution environment to run TPC-H benchmark up to Scale Factor 1000 (SF1000). Evaluated against a rigorous CPU ground truth (DuckDB), our native TPU accelerator achieves state-of-the-art performance, achieving a 7.0x single-device speedup over DuckDB at SF100 and a 68.6x speedup with 16 TPUs at SF1000 (1TB). The results establish TPUs not merely as dense neural compute hardware, but as a highly competitive, massively scalable substrate for the next generation of analytical query processing.

title: Data Provenance Aggregation and Structural Descriptors for Query-Template Identification
summary:
Runtime query similarity identification supports several activities, including workload analysis, identifying recurring behaviour, auditing, debugging, and anomaly detection. Existing methods for evaluating query similarity mostly rely on SQL text, execution plans, or result values but do not account for input data or how results are derived during query execution.
  This paper proposes a novel approach using data provenance for query-template identification. We construct query-level profiles that capture explicit data dependencies, occurrence frequencies, and structural properties by aggregating tuple-level Lineage and Why-provenance across entire query results. We also derive Provenance Structural Descriptors (PSD), which summarise these profiles using a small set of numerical features.
  We evaluate our proposals using these profiles to identify query templates over \(12{,}500\) distinct query instances generated from parametrised TPC-DS query templates. The experimental evaluation shows that query templates can be identified solely from their provenance footprints, and that accuracy improves as more historical data becomes available. It also shows that PSD achieve high classification accuracy with limited training history and low test-processing cost.

title: FuseRAG: Fusing Structure and Evidence into Inference for Cost-Efficient Graph-based RAG
summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) exploits relationships among evidence to support multi-hop question answering. However, conveying retrieved graphs through non-unique linear textual contexts to Large Language Models (LLMs) leads to graph-structure degradation and inefficient KV-cache reuse. Meanwhile, graph-structure order optimization is already NP-hard, and the additional KV-cache reuse objective further complicates the search by introducing potentially conflicting orders. To tackle these issues, we propose FuseRAG, a cost-efficient graph-based RAG framework that shifts most retrieved evidence from explicit textual contexts to latent representations. Our main idea is to separate reusable evidence content from query-aware structural interactions in latent space, while retaining only a few explicit facts as semantic anchors. The resulting latent representations are injected into decoder self-attention, where they reshape attention over evidence and thereby influence hidden states and next-token probabilities. This design preserves graph structure through latent interactions, enables evidence reuse beyond exact token-prefix matching. Experiments on three multi-hop question-answering datasets with Llama-3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B show that FuseRAG improves answer quality while achieving up to 2.7x and 2.2x TTFT speedups over the fastest graph-based baseline, respectively.

title: NL2SQL with Iterative Self-Refinement
summary: Bridging the gap between human intent and machine logic remains a critical challenge in data access for non-technical users, yet Large Language Models (LLMs) remain unreliable: they hallucinate schema elements, generate syntactically invalid queries, or fail to capture user intent. These limitations are especially critical in domains such as insurance, where KPIs, regulatory constraints, and legacy relational systems demand high precision. We introduce a multi-agent, persona-driven NL2SQL framework that combines (1) domain relevance detection, (2) schema-grounded knowledge construction, (3) KPI-aware SQL synthesis, (4) syntax-level self-repair using sqlite execution feedback, and (5) semantic consistency checking via SQL-to-NL reverse engineering. Our system significantly reduces query hallucination and improves semantic fidelity compared to direct LLM prompting. Evaluated on 60 queries (50 from a HuggingFace text-to-SQL dataset and 10 custom domain queries), the system achieves 90% correctness using Mistral across seven coordinated LLM calls showing that this approach can substantially increase the reliability of NL2SQL pipelines in high-stakes environments.

title: An Error Taxonomy for Property Graph Data
summary: Graph data are increasingly used in applications where relationships and topology matter. Yet, compared to tabular data, the notions of data quality and error types for graphs are less established. Tabular error concepts often fail to capture structural properties and context inherent in graph data, hindering systematic quality assessment in graph-based systems. We focus on property graphs (PGs) in graph databases. PGs are often managed without a prescriptive schema, enabling data insertion without explicit validation, while still exhibiting an implicit schema of recurring structural patterns. Irregularities in these patterns may indicate errors, but their interpretation depends on the surrounding graph context. To address these challenges, we provide a systematic view of errors in graph data by proposing a comprehensive graph-specific taxonomy of error types. To position these errors with respect to established work on tabular data quality, we derive a mapping between graph errors and corresponding error notions in tabular data. This mapping highlights which concepts transfer across data models and where structural properties of graphs introduce fundamentally different challenges requiring extensions. Overall, the taxonomy and mapping provide a shared vocabulary for describing, characterizing, comparing, and studying graph data errors, and they lay the groundwork for future work on error detection and repair in graph data.

title: PrairieFire: Igniting High-Throughput Updates in Large-Scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
summary:
Arrays of modern NVMe SSDs are approaching memory in terms of bandwidth while offering much lower cost per gigabyte. Hence, approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) for billion-scale vectors in applications such as recommendation, search, and retrieval-augmented generation increasingly runs on SSD-based systems. Unfortunately, due to the limited update throughput of existing SSD-based solutions, the indexed corpus cannot keep pace with continuous modifications to data and embedding models, thus hindering broader deployment across more scenarios and larger scales.
  The bottleneck lies in CPU-intensive update paths, where foreground insertions incur frequent SSD accesses and background reassignments repeatedly relocate each vector, making high update throughput difficult to achieve even by exhausting available hardware. In this paper, using buffered updates and batched local rebuilds, we develop PrairieFire with cascaded adjustments, concurrency control, and CPU-GPU-SSD cooperation. These co-designs avoid frequent SSD accesses in foreground updates and heavy background reassignments, achieving high update throughput while maintaining excellent search performance.
  Evaluations show that, compared with state-of-the-art systems, PrairieFire can sustain approximately 3-35x update throughput while maintaining approximately 3-5x search throughput simultaneously. It also achieves approximately 1.5-8.7x cost efficiency. PrairieFire has been deployed in RedNote's production environments for two months, improving business metrics by higher freshness without frequent index rebuilds.

title: Joining Large String Collections with Jaro-Winkler Similarity
comment: Accepted for publication in Proc. ACM Manag. Data (PACMMOD / SIGMOD 2027). Please cite the official version: https://doi.org/10.1145/3856354
summary:
The Jaro-Winkler measure, originally developed for U.S.\ Census record linkage, captures similarities between strings and accounts for common typographical variations. Despite its widespread use, finding all string pairs that exceed a given Jaro-Winkler threshold remains challenging as the string collection grows large. Existing algorithms for computing the Jaro-Winkler similarity between two strings are either slow for short strings or require quadratic time and fail to scale to long strings. To reduce the number of string comparisons, state-of-the-art techniques perform an index-nested-loop join on trie-based indexes; however, they have only been evaluated on small datasets and high similarity thresholds. For lower similarity thresholds that are relevant in practice, these techniques incur an excessive number of costly Jaro-Winkler computations.
  We present a novel approach for efficient Jaro-Winkler similarity joins on large string collections. Our solution is based on three key techniques: (1) JUMP is a fast algorithm for computing the Jaro-Winkler similarity between two strings that runs in linear time for bounded alphabets. (2) Dual-bound intersection bitmaps encode strings -- represented as character sets -- into fixed-size bitmaps, which are used to prune candidate string pairs by providing effective bounds on their character overlap; unlike prior bitmap techniques, our bitmaps are equipped with a cost model and adapt to the input data. (3) Our PUMA framework groups strings by prefix to tighten filter conditions, thereby reducing the number of similarity computations. Extensive experiments on large string collections demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms the state of the art, achieving speedups of up to three orders of magnitude.

title: ACED-Bench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Acquire and Act on Causal Evidence
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet we still lack reliable ways to evaluate whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt. A useful evaluation must let agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions, while keeping the environment coherent across repeated observations and interventions and preserving objective ground truth. We introduce ACED-BENCH (Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark), a neuro-symbolic benchmark built around this requirement. The key idea is to separate the readable scientific surface from the formal causal world: LLMs generate natural-language scenarios and task text, while hidden probabilistic graphical models define the causal graph, data-generating process, intervention semantics, validation checks, and oracle answers. This yields scientific worlds that are natural for agents to investigate but exact enough for scalable, programmatic evaluation. The main leaderboard ACED-CORE contains 180 tasks: 60 set-valued causal ancestry/descendancy questions and 120 constrained causal-decision tasks. We also report ACED-QUAL, a 150-question yes/no qualification check using the same hidden-PGM interface. We evaluate seven contemporary LLMs and two earlier-generation models across three active agent designs. ACED-QUAL checks whether agents can use the interface to draw conclusions from evidence, while ACED-CORE tests whether they can decide what evidence to collect and when to commit to an answer. Evidence-ledger analysis localizes failures within the investigation: agents test the wrong intervention, lose relevant evidence, or continue after sufficient evidence has appeared. These results suggest that reliable AI co-scientists need explicit support for experiment design, evidence retention, answer commitment, and stopping.

title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
summary: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against expert solutions on Kaggle competitions. We find that the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy. Our qualitative analysis shows that DS agents generally lack problem solving creativity and domain knowledge, compared to competition-winning data scientists. We believe that principled failure mode analysis, as presented here, should be integral part of agentic DS evaluations, and that the insights we surface will be key in developing trustworthy agentic DS pipelines.

title: JetStream: Generating Verified Query Accelerators for Existing Database Systems
summary: Recent work has shown that LLMs can synthesize highly specialized database systems for fixed workloads, but these systems replace the DBMS's native storage and assume static data: users must migrate their data, often give up ad-hoc queries, and lose acceleration once the data changes. We present JetStream, which instead generates query-specific accelerators that extend an existing DBMS. Given a set of parametrized query templates, a staged agentic workflow synthesizes accelerators that run directly over the DBMS's native tables and may maintain custom auxiliary state, while the DBMS remains responsible for storage, transactions, recovery, and all other queries. A fixed, engine-neutral substrate handles engine-specific hooks and keeps auxiliary state transactionally consistent under writes. JetStream generates two kinds of accelerators: tested accelerators, which may use any optimization and are validated by differential testing, and verified accelerators which trade some performance for a machine-checked proof that every answer satisfies a trusted specification derived from the SQL. On TPC-H at SF=20, JetStream achieves a geomean read speedup over DuckDB ( verified) and retains under a continuous update stream of 10,000 modified rows per second.

title: From GPU Cost Characterization to Memory-Aware Query Execution in Sirius
summary: GPU query performance depends on how an engine represents, moves and reuses data as well as on the kernels that execute its operators. This paper investigates these decisions in Sirius, a GPU-native SQL engine integrated with DuckDB. We begin with a question: which cost information is sufficient to choose a useful execution strategy? A standalone calibration shows that logical byte counts and a simple address-sector estimate fail to predict latency reliably, motivating a cost representation that includes access pattern, placement and reuse. We then evaluate three execution alternatives in Sirius: smaller scan batches, reader-side filter just-in-time compilation, and decoded GPU residency. The first two alternatives fail to improve the tested query. Keeping a fixed column union resident on the GPU improves complete hot query latency on two fixed TPC-H SF1 queries: independent paired measurements give speed ratios of 3.23 for Q6 and 1.73 for Q1. Residency incurs an upfront pin cost of approximately 64 ms, making reuse central to the decision. These results support placement-aware optimization on this workload and identify the measurements needed for an automatic GPU cost model. They do not establish a general cost predictor or a benefit from new kernel fusion.

title: Join Order Enumeration and Optimization for Double-Star and Helix Join Graphs
summary: Join ordering is classic problem in data management. We highlight the connection between structure-specific dynamic programming algorithms and the mathematical enumeration of the possible merge trees from a join graph. We present two case studies, on double-star and helix shaped join graphs, that we believe carry useful techniques for a toolbox of building structure-specific join optimizers. For the double-star case, we show how the enumeration leads directly to a significantly improved search algorithm, whereas for the helix case we show that a algorithm derived from the mathematical enumeration is not necessarily better than structure-agnostic algorithms.

title: Optimize Once, Execute Fast: Latency-Aware Multi-Agent Workflow Learning for Recurrent Queries
summary: Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-based MAS) have shown remarkable success in solving complex tasks by coordinating specialized agents through multi-step workflows. To overcome the high cost and specificity of manually designed workflows, recent research has shifted toward learning them automatically. However, a key limitation remains: while agent calls introduce significant latency due to model inference time and service congestion, most automated methods optimize solely for downstream performance, ignoring execution time (makespan). This issue is amplified when workflows are reused across recurring queries, making latency accumulate over time. This limits deployment in recurrent applications such as AI customer support and AI cloud troubleshooting, where users expect fast responses. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new problem, termed latency-aware workflow generation, where the objective is to minimize workflow makespan while aiming to retain downstream performance. We propose LAWA (Latency-Aware Workflow optimizAtion), a novel framework that reduces makespan via theoretically grounded graph edits targeting critical-path bottlenecks. By unifying a graph generator with this graph-editing procedure, LAWA supports both de novo workflow generation and refinement of existing ones. Empirical results across seven benchmarks demonstrate that LAWA significantly reduces makespan while achieving competitive task performance, supporting efficient reuse of multi-agent workflows for recurrent queries.

title: Bipartite Matching with Few Rounds of Demand Queries
summary: We study the randomised and deterministic demand-query complexity of approximate bipartite matching with few query rounds. The demand-query model, introduced in [Blumrosen and Nisan SICOMP 2009; Nisan SODA 2021], is inspired by combinatorial auctions and welfare maximisation, where an oracle returns the first neighbouring vertex (item) of a vertex u (agent) according to a given permutation pi (preference ordering of the agent over the items). For randomised algorithms, our main result gives a trade-off between the number of rounds k, the per-round query budget q=n^{1+\delta}, and the achievable approximation ratio. Let 1 <= k <= log n, and -1 <= delta <= 1/k. Every k-round randomised algorithm using O(q) demand queries per round has a worst-case expected-size approximation factor of Omega(n^{1/2k-delta/2}/k). Conversely, we give a randomised algorithm achieving approximation factor O(n^{(1-k*delta)/(k+1)}/k) in expectation. For deterministic algorithms, for k*q >= n, we show that the optimal deterministic approximation factor is ~Theta(n^2/(q*k^2)), thereby improving the previous lower bound of [Nisan SODA 2021] by a polynomial factor over a wide range of parameters. In particular, for q=Theta(n), we improve the deterministic round-complexity lower bound for constant-factor approximation from ~Omega(n^{1/3}) to ~Omega(sqrt n). Our algorithms produce matching and vertex-cover certificates; the deterministic trade-off also extends to minimum vertex cover and maximum fractional matching. We extend the randomised upper bounds to the weaker Demand-OR model [Nisan 2021]. We prove a non-adaptive simulation of uniform random-neighbour queries using known techniques, avoiding the O(log n)-round penalty of the trivial binary-search simulation. Consequently, our upper bounds yield the same k-round approximation guarantees using O(q * log^2 n) Demand-OR queries per round.

title: Intelligent Load Balancing and Query Optimization in Distributed Graph Database Architectures
summary: Distributed graph databases have become increasingly important for managing complex relationships in social networks, financial transactions, recommendation systems, knowledge graphs, cybersecurity, and large-scale data analytics. However, distributing graph data across multiple servers introduces significant challenges related to workload imbalance, communication overhead, partition fragmentation, query execution latency, and resource utilization. Traditional load-balancing and query-optimization techniques often struggle with graph workloads because graph structures exhibit irregular connectivity, skewed degree distributions, and highly variable traversal patterns. This research investigates an intelligent framework for load balancing and query optimization in distributed graph database architectures by integrating artificial intelligence, machine learning, graph partitioning, workload prediction, and adaptive query scheduling. The proposed framework combines workload-aware graph partitioning, predictive resource allocation, cost-based query planning, and runtime feedback to improve distributed query performance. It considers graph locality, node centrality, edge distribution, cache utilization, network communication, server capacity, and query complexity when making optimization decisions. An experimental evaluation framework is developed to compare a conventional static architecture with an intelligent adaptive architecture using query latency, throughput, load imbalance, communication overhead, and resource utilization as performance indicators. Illustrative experimental results demonstrate how predictive scheduling and adaptive partitioning could improve throughput, reduce response time, and distribute computational workloads more evenly across participating servers. These results are hypothetical and are intended to demonstrate the proposed methodology rather than represent measurements from an executed benchmark. The research concludes that integrating machine learning with distributed graph processing can provide a foundation for scalable and adaptive database management, particularly when optimization decisions are guided by workload characteristics, real-time system conditions, and measurable performance objectives.

title: When Not to Hint: Adapting an LLM Query Optimizer to a New Database Instance
summary: Query optimization is the problem of determining how to efficiently execute a SQL statement, and errors in a database's cost model can leave a query running orders of magnitude slower than necessary. Recent systems fine-tune large language models to correct these mistakes with a hint (a directive that constrains the optimizer's choices) and supervise the models with labels obtained from executing candidate plans on a single server and recording the fastest. Supervision of this kind is representative of the instance that produced it: under the hint labels released with LLMOpt, a fine-tuned hint generator for PostgreSQL, the Join Order Benchmark runs on our own instance at under half the speed of the default optimizer, and models we fine-tune on the labels similarly underperform. We show that to adapt such a model to a new database instance, full local relabeling and retraining is not required. We relabel 5.8% of training queries with the locally fastest option including not hinting, continue training the model on the result, and a gate based on the default optimizer's cost estimates then selects a sampled hint. On the benchmark, the resulting pipeline opts to hint on roughly a third of queries, achieving a speedup of 1.451× on them and an overall speedup of 1.081×, reliably above both the default optimizer and the foreign-labeled model it starts from.

title: QREF: Improving DeepSearch Agents by Aligning Search with Reasoning via Query Refinement and Evidence Filtering
summary: DeepSearch agents achieve strong performance on complex information-seeking tasks through iterative search and reasoning. However, they often issue intent-misaligned, under-constrained, or redundant search queries, resulting in poor evidence coverage and accumulating retrieval noise. To mitigate these limitations, we propose QREF, a plug-and-play Query Refiner and Evidence Filter. Specifically, the Query Refiner rewrites search queries according to the current reasoning intent while ensuring complementary coverage across each search batch. The Evidence Filter retains evidence relevant to both the current search batch and the reasoning objective, reducing distracting retrieval results. We initialize the Query Refiner with supervised fine-tuning and optimize it through reinforcement learning based on interactions with a real-world web search environment, reducing ineffective queries. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our approach improves the performance of DeepSearch agents across four challenging benchmarks, achieving average relative Pass@1 improvements of 33.55% on WebSailor and 11.04% on TongyiDeepResearch without modifying architectures or retraining their reasoning policies. Compared with the original DeepSearch backbone without QREF, the RL-trained refiner reduces the fraction of query batches that lack discriminative retrieval anchors by 95%. Compared with the SFT-trained refiner, it also lowers the filter-based ineffective query ratio.

title: Digital twin-assisted edge-local query resolution for privacy–utility trade-off in location-based services
summary: Location-Based Services (LBS) generate large volumes of sensitive, location-dependent queries that must be processed under strict and often conflicting constraints of privacy and utility. Existing differential privacy (DP) mechanisms face a fundamental limitation: strong guarantees inject excessive noise and degrade utility, while utility-oriented methods under-protect users. We propose DT-ELR (Digital Twin-assisted Edge-Local Resolution), a framework that jointly optimises disclosure and retrieval utility through two tightly integrated algorithms and an on-device digital twin. Algorithm 1 (SensitivityClassifier) calibrates a monotone geo-indistinguishability budget from a data-derived sensitivity score, validated against a semantic venue-category labelling (AUC 0.81). The digital twin predicts from on-device signals alone whether releasing a query would improve its answer (AUC 0.90); self-sufficient queries are resolved against an on-device venue cache with no release and no budget spent. Algorithm 2 (ClosedFormAllocator) then distributes the remaining budget across released queries in closed form, matching the exact dynamic-programming optimum to within 1%. Experiments on three public check-in corpora — Foursquare-NYC, Gowalla and Brightkite — using an end-to-end nearest-venue retrieval task and three implemented adversaries, show that DT-ELR reduces optimal-inference localization success on sensitive queries from 61.3% to 11.4% on Foursquare-NYC at a matched mean budget, while raising end-to-end retrieval precision from 0.244 under full release to 0.559. Twin-guided release routing outperforms a tuned distance heuristic at every matched release rate, approaching an oracle ceiling of 0.565, and keeps 73% of sensitive queries entirely on the device. Component analysis confirms that each mechanism contributes independently, with edge-local resolution dominant, and the sensitivity model transfers to Gowalla and Brightkite without refitting. Against three recent location-perturbation mechanisms at a matched budget, DT-ELR attains a dominant privacy–utility frontier on all three corpora: higher utility at equal disclosure, and lower disclosure at equal utility.

title: Managing Vector Data for Retrieval Augmented Generation@ Dagstuhl Seminar Summary
summary: This report summarizes discussions that took place in the context of a Dagstuhl seminar1 to explore the emerging paradigm of AI-native databases designed to support agentic workflows and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with robust database abstractions. The central synthesis of the Dagstuhl discussions is the necessary evolution of databases from passive vector stores into active data-native agentic harnesses that orchestrate AI reasoning and task-centric execution. A recurring lesson across keynotes and working groups is that achieving mission-critical reliability requires integrating AI primitives, such as embeddings, model inference, and semantic operators, as first-class citizens while maintaining traditional database guarantees like transactional consistency, explainability, and cost-aware optimization. This transition necessitates a structured approach to agent memory (spanning episodic, semantic, and procedural scales) and a shift toward adaptive, iterative execution models that go beyond static query planning to accommodate the stochastic nature of foundation models. There is a community consensus that reliability, responsibility, and security (specifically addressing compositional leakage) must be treated as end-to-end concerns supported by holistic benchmarks that evaluate the entire quality chain from retrieval to autonomous action.

title: TraHist: Fast and Accurate Cardinality Estimation for Trajectory Data (Extended Version)
summary: Cardinality estimation is fundamental for query optimization in database systems. Histogram-based estimators are widely used for their simplicity and efficiency but rely on point-centric partitioning that assumes record independence. This assumption breaks in trajectory data, where records from the same moving object show strong spatiotemporal dependencies. Conventional axis-aligned histograms therefore fragment trajectories across partition boundaries, leading to overestimation through duplicate counting. This error reflects a structural limitation of partition boundaries that are misaligned with trajectory-induced density patterns. To this end, we propose TraHist, a histogram-based estimator approximating density-aligned partitioning via efficient grid-based propagation. TraHist builds density-adaptive rectilinear buckets to preserve trajectory continuity and local density coherence while keeping histogram efficiency. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets show that TraHist reduces estimation error by over 20x relative to the strongest competing estimator in query regimes where trajectory fragmentation is a dominant source of estimation error, while maintaining sub-millisecond query latency and competitive construction cost.

title: A conceptual and logical modeling methodology for data warehousing
summary: Traditional data warehouse (DW) design approaches often represent measures, granularity hierarchies, and process semantics implicitly, limiting traceability between analytical requirements and logical schema structures. This paper proposes a conceptual and logical modeling methodology (CLMM) that integrates entity–relationship modeling with business–process modeling and treats measures, granularity hierarchies, and process states as explicit conceptual constructs. A formal metamodel, rule-based conceptual-to-logical transformations, and validation constraints are defined to support multi-grain periodic snapshots and process-driven accumulating snapshots. The evaluation covers transformation correctness, semantic error detection, fair query performance comparison, and empirical validation of the process-driven pattern using a real-world event log. The results show that CLMM consistently generates the expected logical structures and detects controlled modeling inconsistencies. Under equivalent schema configurations, CLMM achieves query performance comparable to a manually designed Kimball schema, while improvements over a basic star schema are mainly attributable to multi-granularity pre-aggregation. The results support the methodological feasibility and reproducibility of CLMM, and distributed large-scale scalability remains outside the scope of the present study.

title: Evaluating the ROI of Self-Service Business Intelligence Tools Across Functional Business Units: A Non-Linear Empirical Assessment Framework
summary: Self-Service Business Intelligence (SSBI) tools have revolutionized corporate decisionmaking by decentralizing analytics capabilities from central IT departments to end-user functional business units. However, quantifying the financial Return on Investment (ROI) and operational efficacy of SSBI platforms across heterogeneous organizational functions remains a major challenge due to unobserved productivity gains, dynamic software licensing structures, and data governance overheads. This paper presents a novel multi-dimensional non-linear evaluation model engineered to capture both financial and non-financial metrics associated with SSBI adoption. Utilizing an empirical enterprise dataset tracking 8,500 active SSBI users across Finance, Marketing, Operations, and Sales across 45 enterprise organizations between 2018 and 2023, our non-linear evaluation framework demonstrates that SSBI investments yield an aggregate ROI of 184.2% over a 36-month horizon, reducing average Time-to-Insight (TTI) by 74.5%. Grounded in non-linear predictive modeling methodologies and strategic enterprise governance principles, we establish that ROI scaling follows a non-linear trajectory governed by user autonomy and governance maturity. The paper incorporates an exhaustive quantitative synthesis incorporating 10 data tables, 10 mathematical behavior graphs, and 20 visually unique chart architectures mapping organizational analytics performance.

title: LLM-Augmented Semantic Edge Intelligence in Wireless Sensor Networks and IoT: A Review-Led Evidence Synthesis and Conceptual Framework
summary: Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) increasingly support sensing-to-decision loops in which the value of a transmission depends on task utility, freshness, uncertainty, privacy, and safety rather than on bit fidelity alone. This article presents a review-led evidence synthesis and, as a secondary contribution, an author-proposed conceptual framework; it does not report a validated control algorithm. The review analyzes a 178-record evidence corpus, complemented by seven separately logged mathematical-outlook references, across WSN and IoT foundations, semantic communication, TinyML and split inference, federated learning, generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), digital twins, wireless foundation models, and language-model-assisted operations. The supplementary materials release a machine-readable extraction sheet with one row per record, a field codebook, a reference and screening ledger, qualification and completeness audits, and an integrity manifest. A work qualifies as LLM-augmented semantic edge intelligence only when an identifiable large language model (LLM) consumes task-relevant WSN/IoT state or operator intent and can affect sensing, communication, diagnosis, resource allocation, or control through a typed and auditable path. Under this boundary, only one retained work supplies direct E2 simulation evidence of an LLM-mediated communication or control path. Most LLM/RAG evidence is bridging or adjacent and remains at E0–E2. The synthesis therefore distinguishes the roles and maturity of the component technologies instead of treating them as an interchangeable stack. It identifies bounded examples of LLM/RAG utility in communication-policy generation, cross-task networking adaptation, global evidence synthesis, tool orchestration, and natural-language formulation for an external solver. It does not support a general claim of superiority over rules, exact optimization, structured retrieval, or task-specific machine learning and reinforcement learning. To translate the documented gaps into testable requirements, the article proposes an IoT-native reference architecture, a seven-axis taxonomy, a threat model, a formal synthesis and selection/cost model, typed cross-layer interface contracts, and an eight-phase benchmark protocol. These normative artifacts are proposed by the author. They are not established methods extracted from the corpus, consensus standards, a deployable solver or controller, or experimentally validated results. An explicitly hypothetical wildfire-monitoring case makes the formalism inspectable: it defines semantic distortion, normalizes and elicits the penalty weights, evaluates a finite candidate set under hard constraints, applies the non-dominance and LLM-admission rules, reports switch-point sensitivity, and exercises one LLM-to-optimizer interface contract. Its values are tutorial inputs, not measurements. A provenance audit separates cited evidence, author-defined review and coding constructs, conventional notation, and proposed framework artifacts. Each contribution is linked to measurable outcomes and a minimum support condition, but these quantities define future tests rather than imply new performance gains. An LLM is retained only when it closes a declared open-vocabulary or heterogeneous-knowledge capability gap, satisfies hard energy, deadline, privacy, safety, and verifier constraints, and provides positive incremental value over the strongest feasible simpler baseline. Resource-constrained nodes continue to handle sensing, routing, medium access control, and lightweight inference. Grounded LLM/RAG components operate at gateway, edge, cloud, or digital-twin …

title: Constrained Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in Imagination
summary: Predicting cost in a multi-agent world model moves most constrained policy updates into imagination: the stronger model-free baseline needs to times CA-MAMBA's interactions on the median SMAC configuration, and CA-MAMBA earns to times the baselines' MAMuJoCo reward at equal budget. In controlled tests on one task per benchmark, pricing the model's cost advantages at parity more than halves a cost-blind learner's cost and meets a tight continuous-control limit the learned multiplier misses, suggesting the model's cost estimates are not the bottleneck.

title: An interpretable machine learning framework for retrospective attribution of hospitalization costs in patients with chronic kidney disease
summary: Hospitalization costs vary substantially among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), yet the factors underlying this heterogeneity are not fully understood. We developed an interpretable machine learning framework to retrospectively characterize differences in hospitalization costs among patients with CKD and externally evaluated its performance. The study included 3,017 hospitalizations from one tertiary hospital and 2,708 hospitalizations from another tertiary hospital for external validation. Patients were analyzed separately according to kidney transplant status, including non-transplant (n = 2,435) and transplant (n = 582) groups. Multiple machine learning and conventional statistical models were compared using temporal holdout testing, external validation, and sensitivity analyses. LightGBM performed best in the non-transplant group (R² = 0.7060), whereas XGBoost performed best in the transplant group (R² = 0.6235). External validation yielded R² values of 0.5921 and 0.5513, respectively. Model interpretation identified length of stay, treatment-related features, age, and selected laboratory measures as prominent contributors to predicted costs, with nonlinear patterns and substantial patient-level heterogeneity. This framework provides a transparent approach for retrospective hospitalization cost attribution and case-mix analysis in CKD.

title: Hit Rate Is Not Value: When Cache Metrics Mislead in Tiered LLM KV-Cache Persistence
summary: We set out to beat LRU at evicting persisted LLM KV caches at different tiers (GPU VRAM, NVMe, Object storage) with a learned policy and failed at this. Across three synthetic workloads, two served architectures and a replay of the Azure LLM inference trace, LRU wins at cache hit rate every single time. However, if we measure in terms of GPU time actually saved, LRU delivers the least value of any policy we test on enterprise level of traffic. Here, a value density policy concedes 21 hit rate points to LRU by saving 1.99 times as much compute and still 1.15 times once we correct the architecture the same analysis exposes. Hit rate assumes every hit is worth the same, but KV caches vary in size and compute time. A hit below the context length N* is worth nothing, and above it the savings grow superlinearly. Both effects depend on N*, and the largest factor they expose is provisioning, not policy: deleting a tier that cannot justify the restore time is worth 3.6 times at identical capacity. A ground truth ablation study isolates the failure where two clairvoyant policies that both cache perfectly with 100% hit rate still deliver significantly different value in terms of GPU compute time.

title: G-Merging: Merging Models within O (1) Memory Cost via Gossip Approach
summary: Multitask model merging is essential for enabling a single model to perform multiple tasks simultaneously, ad dressing scalability and efficiency challenges in machine learning systems. While existing methods enhance the performance of traditional approaches like Task Arithmetic, they require substantial GPU memory. For example, AdaMerging enhances performance by autonomously learning merging coefficients through entropy minimization on unlabeled test samples. How ever, it necessitates loading all K models into GPU memory, leading to substantial memory overhead as the number and size of models increase. To overcome these limitations and achieve both high performance and low GPU memory usage, we introduce G-Merging, a decentralized multitask model merging approach. G-Merging distributes models across multiple de vices arranged in a ring topology and performs merging by combining each model only with its adjacent neighbors. Through iterative merging processes, all models converge into a unified multitask learning (MTL) model. Importantly, our method ensures that each device stores no more than four models at any time, regardless of the total number of models being merged. This memory reduction is obtained by trading additional local merging rounds and runtime for a lower per-device GPU memory requirement. Experimental results demonstrate that G-Merging requires about 20% of the post-cleanup resident GPU memory of AdaMerging without compromising accuracy when merging 20 CLIP-ViT-B/32 models, reducing the resident memory cost from 8.2GB to 1.7GB.

title: APPLICATION AND ARCHITECTURAL APPROACHES OF CLOUD-BASED LABORATORIES IN HIGHER EDUCATION
summary: Universities increasingly turn to cloud computing to deliver laboratory work, yet adoption is often fragmented: individual instructors use separate services that are not connected to the institution's learning management system (LMS), and resource costs go unplanned. This article systematizes architectural approaches to cloud-based laboratories in higher education. Laboratory courses are grouped into four categories according to four requirement dimensions: isolation, real-time interaction, resource intensity and the need for physical equipment. For each category a suitable architecture is identified: container-based PaaS environments for programming and data analysis, isolated IaaS environments for networking and cybersecurity, remotely operated physical test benches supported by edge nodes for electronics and automation, and hybrid simulation-plus-bench setups for the natural sciences. The article proposes a three-tier integration model that connects the university LMS, a laboratory platform and computing resources, providing single sign-on via LTI 1.3, on-demand provisioning of individual lab environments and automatic grade return through LTI Assignment and Grade Services. A per-student cost model, a four-stage implementation roadmap with measurable transition criteria, and a set of technical, economic and pedagogical evaluation metrics are also developed. The results can guide universities, particularly regional institutions in Azerbaijan, in modernizing their laboratory infrastructure.

title: Learning Warm Starts for the Simplex Method from Measured Solver Cost
summary: Learned warm starts for the simplex method build starting bases using predictions of which variables will be basic at optimality. Prior work has shown that starting bases predicted by graph neural networks can sharply reduce iteration counts, but the time saved may fall well short of the iterations saved. On 25 classes of linear programs (LPs), we find that a strong supervised basis predictor removes two thirds of the dual simplex's iterations but only a third of its time. Two effects explain the gap: the iterations removed by a good start tend to be cheap, and closeness to an optimal basis does not rank starts by cost. We prove that two starts with equal overlap with an optimal basis and equal pivot counts can differ in linear-algebra work by a factor that grows with the square root of the number of rows. Empirically, across the starts of one LP, the pivot count explains 71% of the variance of log solve time, while the CPU instruction count explains 98.5%. We introduce CostStart, which uses supervised prediction for the basis and trains a small policy on measured instruction counts to choose, per LP, how many predicted columns to use, which algorithm and pricing rule to run, and whether to warm-start at all. On unseen LPs of the training classes, including LPs four times the training size, CostStart roughly halves the solve time relative to the solver's default start and is 1.4 to 2.2 times as fast as two published methods retrained on the same data.

title: X-RIC: An Agentic RAN-Intelligent Controller Benchmark for Enhancing Reinforcement Learning
summary: The O-RAN ALLIANCE introduces architectural flexibility through disaggregation and AI-driven control. While the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) enables centralized optimization, current AI approaches lack reasoning capabilities and explainability. We propose eXplainable RIC (X-RIC), a novel framework integrating agentic AI into O-RAN architectures. X-RIC combines reactive Reinforcement Learning (RL) with strategic agentic reasoning through: (i) automated Behavioral Cloning (BC) using domain heuristics for sample-efficient training, (ii) a Telecom Language Model (TLM), a transformer-based reasoning module providing contextual abstraction and interpretability, and (iii) closed-loop co-adaptation within the Near-RT RIC control loop enabling continuous policy refinement. To ensure deployment readiness, we introduce BARX (Benchmarking Agentic Reasoning for RAN), a domain-specific evaluation framework assessing agentic control across latency, compliance, and determinism metrics. We validate X-RIC on SLA-aware network slicing in simulation and O-RAN-compliant testbed deployments. X-RIC achieves 89% operational cost reduction while maintaining SLA compliance, converging 75% faster with 50% fewer training steps and 46% lower variance.

title: When Not to Hint: Adapting an LLM Query Optimizer to a New Database Instance
summary: Query optimization is the problem of determining how to efficiently execute a SQL statement, and errors in a database's cost model can leave a query running orders of magnitude slower than necessary. Recent systems fine-tune large language models to correct these mistakes with a hint (a directive that constrains the optimizer's choices) and supervise the models with labels obtained from executing candidate plans on a single server and recording the fastest. Supervision of this kind is representative of the instance that produced it: under the hint labels released with LLMOpt, a fine-tuned hint generator for PostgreSQL, the Join Order Benchmark runs on our own instance at under half the speed of the default optimizer, and models we fine-tune on the labels similarly underperform. We show that to adapt such a model to a new database instance, full local relabeling and retraining is not required. We relabel 5.8% of training queries with the locally fastest option including not hinting, continue training the model on the result, and a gate based on the default optimizer's cost estimates then selects a sampled hint. On the benchmark, the resulting pipeline opts to hint on roughly a third of queries, achieving a speedup of 1.451× on them and an overall speedup of 1.081×, reliably above both the default optimizer and the foreign-labeled model it starts from.

title: From Long Context to Selective Memory: A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models
summary: Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. Existing work on prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory is usually discussed in isolation, leaving the flow of information between storage and computation insufficiently understood. This survey reframes long-context compression as a memory-management problem for allocating inference-time resources. We distinguish compute-active memory, which directly participates in model computation, from compute-inactive memory, which lies outside the computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten, and we characterize offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and precomputed KV states as intermediate states on the activation path. On this basis, we formulate writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as state transitions within an information lifecycle, and introduce a budgeted cost model that places these operations in a single cost account. The resulting framework unifies short-term context compression, long-term memory management, and the transitions between them, and shows that the central challenge is not merely reducing information volume but deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form. We further summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and argue that future research should move from static, pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.
